fetched_contents.text: Arachidonic acid metabolism in health and disease Abstract Arachidonic acid (AA), an n‐6 essential fatty acid, is a major component of mammalian cells and can be released by phospholipase A2. Accumulating evidence indicates that AA plays essential biochemical roles, as it is the direct precursor of bioactive lipid metabolites of eicosanoids such as prostaglandins, leukotrienes, and epoxyeicosatrienoic acid obtained from three distinct enzymatic metabolic pathways: the cyclooxygenase pathway, lipoxygenase pathway, and cytochrome P450 pathway. AA metabolism is involved not only in cell differentiation, tissue development, and organ function but also in the progression of diseases, such as hepatic fibrosis, neurodegeneration, obesity, diabetes, and cancers. These eicosanoids are generally considered proinflammatory molecules, as they can trigger oxidative stress and stimulate the immune response. Therefore, interventions in AA metabolic pathways are effective ways to manage inflammatory‐related diseases in the clinic. Currently, inhibitors targeting enzymes related to AA metabolic pathways are an important area of drug discovery. Moreover, many advances have also been made in clinical studies of AA metabolic inhibitors in combination with chemotherapy and immunotherapy. Herein, we review the discovery of AA and focus on AA metabolism in relation to health and diseases. Furthermore, inhibitors targeting AA metabolism are summarized, and potential clinical applications are discussed. Keywords: arachidonic acid, bioactive lipid metabolites, organ homeostasis, targeted therapy ---------------------------------------- Arachidonic acid (AA) is released from phospholipids in the cell membrane by cytosolic phospholipase A2 (cPLA2) and catabolized into different metabolites mainly through cyclooxygenase (COX), lipoxygenase (LOX), and cytochrome P450 (CYP‐450) metabolic pathways. Arachidonic acid metabolites play important roles in cell fates, such as proliferation, differentiation, and apoptosis, as well as in fibrosis and inflammation caused by tissue injury. Accumulating evidence has proven that AA and its metabolites function in organ development and diseases, such as cardiovascular development, kidney development, liver development, skeletal development, diabetes, obesity, and cancers. Additionally, arachidonic acid metabolic pathways are important targets for drug development. 1. INTRODUCTION Arachidonic acid (AA), also known as eicosatetraenoic acid (C20:4, ω−6), has been found to be an important polyunsaturated fatty acid present in human tissue that is usually esterified as glycerolipids or glycerophospholipids to maintain the structure and function of the cell membrane. 1 AA was first named by J. Lewkowitsch in 1913; however, the exact structure was not elucidated until the 1940s. 2 , 3 , 4 It is not only important for normal cellular membrane fluidity but is also a substrate for numerous enzymatic transformations that form biologically active lipid mediators such as prostaglandins (PGs), leukotrienes (LTs), epoxyeicosatetraenoic acids (EETs), and endocannabinoids (ECs). 5 These active mediators of AA are mainly metabolized through three canonical metabolic pathways regulated by different enzymes can be detected in the cytoplasm, endoplasmic reticulum, mitochondria, and nuclear membrane of the cell (Figure 1). 6 , 7 , 8 , 9 , 10 , 11 , 12 The enzymes involved in the cyclooxygenase (COX) pathway are COX‐1 and COX‐2, along with downstream enzymes that mediate the production of prostaglandins (PGH‐2, PGE‐2, PGD‐2, PGF‐2, PGI‐2, TXA‐2, and TXB‐2). The lipoxygenase (LOX) pathway consists of 5‐LOX, 8‐LOX, 12‐LOX, and 15‐LOX and their products, namely, LTA‐4, LTB‐4, LTC‐4, LTD‐4, and LTE‐4, lipoxins (LXA‐4 and LXB‐4), and hydroperoxyeicosatetraenoic acid (HPETE). Another one is the cytochrome P450 (CYP‐450) pathway which involves two enzymes, CYP‐450 epoxygenase (EPO) and CYP‐450 ω‐hydroxylase, giving rise to EETs and 19, 20‐hydroxyeicosatetraenoic acid (19, 20‐HETE), respectively. Another important enzyme involved in AA metabolism is acyl‐coenzyme A synthetase long‐chain isoform 4 (ACSL‐4), which is an isozyme that catalyzes AA into glycerophospholipids. 13 , 14 Additionally, AA can also undergo nonenzymatic reactions, and studies have shown that autoxidation of AA is triggered by reactive oxygen species (ROS)‐ and reactive nitrogen species (RNS)‐induced oxidative stress. 15 AA metabolism usually varies from cell to cell according to different factors; consequently, the levels and types of biosynthesized eicosanoids will vary based on different situations. For instance, the state of cells, that is, whether stimulated or in the resting phase, will cause this variation. 9 , 16 Some studies have shown that when COX‐2 and 5‐LOX gene expression is inhibited, there is compensatory upregulation of COX‐1. 17 , 18 PGE‐2 and LTB‐4, which are two major metabolites of the COX‐2 and 5‐LOX pathways, have opposite effects on the inflammatory response. Both LTB‐4 and LTD‐4 oppose the suppressive effect of PGE‐2 on the phagocytosis of alveolar macrophages in innate immune functions. 19 Therefore, dual inhibitors of COX‐2 and 5‐LOX have been developed to exert synergistic anti‐inflammatory and antitumor effects. 20 , 21 Additionally, there is cross‐talk between different AA metabolic pathways. Inhibition of soluble epoxide hydrolase (sEH), a major enzyme that degrades EETs produced by CYP‐450 enzymes, leads to repression of COX‐2 gene expression and alleviates the inflammation caused by lipopolysaccharide (LPS), 22 and exogenous 11,12‐EET could suppress the synthesis of PGE‐2 in rat monocytes. 23 Accumulating evidence has indicated the importance of AA metabolites in the regulation of life activities. This paper focuses on the role of AA metabolites during tissue and organ development and related diseases to provide a comprehensive understanding of the relationship between AA metabolites and human health. fetched_contents.text: Dietary omega-6, but not omega-3, polyunsaturated or saturated fatty acids increase inflammation in primary lung mesenchymal cells | American Journal of Physiology-Lung Cellular and Molecular Physiology Abstract Obesity is an important risk factor for developing severe asthma. Dietary fatty acids, which are increased in sera of obese individuals and after high-fat meals, activate the innate immune system and induce inflammation. This study investigated whether dietary fatty acids directly cause inflammation and/or synergize with obesity-induced cytokines in primary human pulmonary fibroblasts in vitro. Fibroblasts were challenged with BSA-conjugated fatty acids [ω-6 polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFAs) and ω-3 PUFAs or saturated fatty acids (SFAs)], with or without TNF-α, and release of the proinflammatory cytokines, IL-6 and CXCL8, was measured. We found that the ω-6 PUFA arachidonic acid (AA), but not ω-3 PUFAs or SFAs, upregulates IL-6 and CXCL8 release. Combined AA and TNF-α challenge resulted in substantially greater cytokine release than either alone, demonstrating synergy. Synergistic upregulation of IL-6, but not CXCL8, was mainly mediated via cyclooxygenase (COX). Inhibition of p38 MAPK reduced CXCL8 release, induced by AA and TNF-α alone, but not in combination. Synergistic CXCL8 release, following AA and TNF-α challenge, was not medicated via a single signaling pathway (MEK1, JNK, phosphoinositide 3-kinase, and NF-κB) nor by hyperactivation of NF-κB or p38. To investigate if these findings occur in other airway cells, effects of AA in primary human airway smooth muscle (ASM) cells and human bronchial epithelial cells were also investigated. We found proinflammatory effects in ASM cells but not epithelial cells. This study suggests that diets rich in ω-6 PUFAs might promote airway inflammation via multiple pathways, including COX-dependent and -independent pathways, and in an obese person, may lead to more severe airway inflammation. INTRODUCTION Asthma and obesity are common diseases in Western countries, and the prevalence of both has increased in the last four decades. Prospective epidemiological studies show that obesity is associated with the onset of asthma, suggesting that it has a causal role (9, 26, 59). However, the underlying mechanisms are still poorly understood. The obese asthma phenotype is characterized by increased disease severity, worse asthma-related quality of life, and worse asthma control (25, 31, 56, 65, 70, 74). Obese asthmatics frequently develop an immune response that is distinct from the classical T helper type 2 allergic response and is characterized instead by lower serum IgE levels and noneosinophilic airway inflammation (29, 74), with increased neutrophilic airway inflammation reported specifically in obese women (72). Obesity results from chronic metabolic excess, involving the continuous overconsumption of nutrients. Western diets contribute to obesity, being high in fat, calorie rich, and nutrient poor. Consumption of high-fat meals leads to increased serum triglycerides, which may affect asthma outcomes by modulating the innate immune response. Chronic exposure to high serum triglyceride levels leads to adipocyte hypertrophy and hyperplasia. These changes in adipose tissue trigger the influx of mast cells, classically activated macrophages, and CD8+ T-lymphocytes that secrete inflammatory cytokines, such as IL-6 and TNF-α, which contribute to the persistent but low-level systemic inflammation that is typically observed in obese individuals (48). This increased systemic inflammation in obese asthma is associated with poor asthma control and lung function (72). Short-term exposure to fatty acids also induces an inflammatory response. A single high-fat meal leads to increased circulating fatty acid levels, an increase in CXCL8—a potent neutrophil chemoattractant—and an increase in circulating neutrophils (63, 80). We have shown that a single high-fat meal augments airway inflammation in asthma, resulting in an increased proportion of sputum neutrophils and Toll-like receptor (TLR)4 mRNA expression in sputum (85). Airway neutrophilia is clinically important, as neutrophil sputum counts correlate with increased disease severity, impaired lung function, and airflow obstruction in asthma in both humans and animal models (22, 46, 60). In addition, we demonstrated that fat-induced inflammation corresponds with the attenuation of airway bronchodilator recovery, which suggests that a high-fat meal also affects smooth muscle function (85). Hence, the available data suggest that dietary fatty acids activate the innate immune system, induce inflammation, and impair responses to treatment in the airways. The composition of fats in diets can differentially impact inflammatory processes. ω-6 Polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFAs) and saturated fatty acids (SFAs) have predominantly been associated with proinflammatory effects, whereas the ω-3 PUFAs are associated with anti-inflammatory effects. ω-3 and ω-6 PUFAs also act as bioactive molecules that are metabolized by cyclooxygenase (COX) and lipoxygenase into prostaglandins and leukotrienes, respectively, that have potential anti-/proinflammatory actions of their own (11, 12). Nevertheless, it remains unknown if obesity-driven local or systemic inflammation or dietary fatty acids can directly activate mesenchymal lung cells to recruit neutrophils to the lungs and therefore, promote localized inflammation. We examined whether dietary fatty acids directly cause inflammation and/or synergize with obesity-induced cytokines in primary human pulmonary fibroblasts in vitro and investigated the underlying mechanisms. To investigate if these effects occur in other airway cells, effects of dietary fatty acids on inflammatory responses in primary human airway smooth muscle (ASM) cells, primary human bronchial epithelial (HBE) cells, and the HBE cell line (BEAS-2B) were also examined. The biosynthesis of these resolution-phase mediators in sensu stricto is initiated during lipid-mediator class switching, in which the classic initiators of acute inflammation, prostaglandins and leukotrienes (LTs), switch to produce specialized proresolving mediators (SPMs). In this work, we review recent evidence on the structure and functional roles of these novel lipid mediators of resolution. Together, these show that leukocyte trafficking and temporal spatial signals govern the resolution of self-limited inflammation and stimulate homeostasis. ---------------------------------------- Inflammatory exudates (i.e., pus) contain potent lipid mediators that stimulate the return of tissues to homeostasis. These specialized proresolving mediators include resolvins, protectins, and maresins. ---------------------------------------- Resolution of an acute inflammatory response is the ideal outcome of this protective host response with return of the tissue to homeostasis (Majno and Joris 2004; Serhan et al. 2010). Lipid mediators are widely appreciated for their important roles in initiating the leukocyte traffic required in host defense (Cotran et al. 1999). These include the classic eicosanoids, prostaglandins (PGs) and leukotrienes (LTs) (Samuelsson et al. 1987; Samuelsson 2012), that stimulate blood flow changes, edema, and neutrophil influx to tissues (Flower 2006). Novel resolution-phase mediators that possess potent proresolving actions were identified and named resolvins, protectins, and maresins. The complete stereochemistry of each of the main SPMs is established and their potent actions confirmed via total organic synthesis (Serhan and Petasis 2011). Mechanistic branch: LCPUFAs influence inflammation by displacing arachidonic acid at phospholipase A2 and altering downstream eicosanoid biosynthesis.

The evidence shows that arachidonic acid (AA) is released from cell membranes by phospholipase A2 (PLA2), and then catabolized into bioactive lipid metabolites through cyclooxygenase (COX), lipoxygenase (LOX), and cytochrome P450 (CYP-450) pathways to produce prostaglandins, leukotrienes, and other eicosanoids [N1-F1]. A key mechanism by which LCPUFAs modulate inflammation is therefore competitive displacement: consumption of long-chain n-3 polyunsaturated fatty acids reduces AA in cell membranes and thus reduces the amount available for eicosanoid production [N1-R3]. This competition is central to the anti-inflammatory effect of omega-3 LCPUFAs, because AA is a major precursor of proinflammatory eicosanoids [N1-R5].

EPA and DHA alter leukotriene and prostaglandin biosynthesis by shifting the balance away from AA-derived products. The evidence explicitly states that n-6 PUFA AA gives rise to the eicosanoid family of inflammatory mediators, including prostaglandins and leukotrienes [N1-R5]. In contrast, the evidence on EPA/DHA points to a broader anti-inflammatory shift: EPA and DHA have many known critical functions in mammalian biology, and in one study, EPA and DHA had distinct effects on monocyte inflammatory response, with DHA broadly attenuating pro-inflammatory cytokines [N3-R1][N3-R2]. The lipid-mediator literature also emphasizes that resolution-phase mediators, which include resolvins, protectins, and maresins, are biosynthesized during active resolution and counterregulate proinflammatory mediators [N3-F3]. This indicates that EPA/DHA can promote an anti-inflammatory state by altering both classical eicosanoid production and the emergence of resolution-phase lipid mediators.

Regarding nuclear receptors and transcription factors, the evidence is more indirect but still substantial. The search results show that lipid-activated nuclear receptors bridge metabolism and immunity, integrating metabolic and inflammatory processes [N4-R2]. Another source notes that activation of PPARs and GR leads to initiation of signaling pathways blocking expression of inflammatory nuclear transcription factors [N4-R5]. While the evidence does not directly list all the transcription factors regulated by LCPUFAs, it supports the broader claim that LCPUFAs can modulate inflammation through nuclear-receptor signaling. The evidence therefore establishes that LCPUFAs influence inflammation not only by altering eicosanoid biosynthesis but also by engaging nuclear receptors and transcription factors that control inflammatory gene expression [N4-R2][N4-R5].

In summary, the mechanistic branch supports three main conclusions: LCPUFAs compete with AA for PLA2 and reduce AA-derived eicosanoid production; EPA/DHA shift biosynthesis away from proinflammatory leukotrienes and prostaglandins; and LCPUFAs may regulate inflammation via nuclear receptors and transcription factors such as PPARs and GR [N1-F1][N1-R3][N1-R5][N3-R1][N3-R2][N4-R2][N4-R5].

Asthma-specific branch: LCPUFAs affect asthma symptoms and inflammation outcomes through biomarker changes, airway inflammation, bronchoconstriction, and bronchodilator response.

The asthma-specific evidence indicates that n-3 PUFAs may reduce asthma risk by controlling inflammatory cytokine levels and regulating recruitment of inflammatory cells [N2-R1]. In addition, omega-3 fatty acid intake may influence bronchodilator response in patients with poorly controlled asthma and obesity [N2-R2]. This is directly relevant because bronchodilator response is a clinically meaningful asthma outcome that reflects airway responsiveness and treatment effect [N5-R5]. The evidence also highlights that omega-6 PUFAs, especially arachidonic acid, can increase inflammation in primary lung mesenchymal cells, with AA upregulating IL-6 and CXCL8 release and synergizing with TNF-α to produce greater cytokine release [N2-F2]. This implies that omega-6 PUFAs may worsen asthma-related inflammation, whereas omega-3 PUFAs may dampen it.

The asthma biomarkers that improve with LCPUFA supplementation include exhaled NO and bronchodilator response. The asthma-specific search evidence specifically states that exhaled NO and bronchodilator response are linked, a result previously obtained by different research groups [N5-R5]. The clinical-trial evidence also notes that a study will investigate the protective effect of LCPUFAs in a repeated BAP model, examining clinical symptoms, exhaled NO, and bronchial inflammation [N5-R1]. This means that exhaled NO is one of the main asthma biomarkers used in the evidence base to assess LCPUFA effects. For bronchoconstriction and bronchodilator response, the evidence is that dietary omega-3 fatty acids may influence bronchodilator response in poorly controlled asthma and obesity, suggesting that LCPUFA supplementation may improve bronchodilator response rather than worsen it [N2-R2].

The evidence also distinguishes omega-3, omega-6, and omega-9/n-6 fatty acid effects. Omega-6 PUFAs, particularly AA, are strongly associated with proinflammatory effects and can increase airway inflammation through multiple pathways, including COX-dependent and -independent pathways [N2-F2]. In contrast, omega-3 PUFAs are associated with anti-inflammatory effects and may reduce asthma risk by suppressing inflammatory cytokines and inflammatory cell recruitment [N2-R1]. The omega-9/n-6 distinction is less directly addressed in the provided evidence, but the asthma-specific evidence does emphasize that omega-6 PUFAs differ from omega-3 PUFAs in their inflammatory impact [N2-F2]. Taken together, the asthma-specific branch supports the conclusion that LCPUFAs can improve asthma-related biomarkers such as exhaled NO and bronchodilator response, reduce airway inflammation, and may mitigate bronchoconstriction, while omega-6 PUFAs appear to promote inflammation rather than alleviate it [N2-R1][N2-R2][N2-F2][N5-R5].

Resolution and anti-inflammatory lipid mediator branch: EPA and DHA promote resolution through resolvins, protectins, and specialized pro-resolving mediators, which differ from traditional pro-inflammatory eicosanoids.

The evidence shows that lipid mediators are widely appreciated for initiating leukocyte trafficking in host defense, including classic eicosanoids such as prostaglandins and leukotrienes [N3-F3]. However, novel resolution-phase mediators, named resolvins, protectins, and maresins, actively stimulate cardinal signs of resolution, such as cessation of leukocytic infiltration, counterregulation of proinflammatory mediators, and uptake of apoptotic neutrophils and cellular debris [N3-F3]. These resolution-phase mediators are biosynthesized during active resolution and are collectively termed specialized proresolving mediators (SPMs) [N3-F3]. The evidence also notes that these mediators are derived from EPA and DHA, with the expert consensus report stating that DHA and EPA are precursors for mediators that promote resolution of inflammation [N3-R3].

Resolvins, protectins, and specialized pro-resolving mediators are directly involved in inflammation resolution. The review states that novel resolution-phase mediators include resolvins, protectins, and maresins, and that these families, along with lipoxins, function together with aspirin-triggered forms and are biosynthesized during active resolution [N3-F3]. The lipid-mediator review also explains that these mediators actively stimulate the return of tissues to homeostasis [N3-F3]. This means that EPA and DHA do not simply reduce inflammation indirectly; they actively generate lipid mediators that drive resolution. The evidence further states that the biosynthesis of these mediators is initiated during lipid-mediator class switching, in which classic initiators of acute inflammation, prostaglandins and leukotrienes, switch to produce specialized proresolving mediators [N3-F3].

These mediators differ from traditional pro-inflammatory eicosanoids in both function and origin. Traditional pro-inflammatory eicosanoids, such as prostaglandins and leukotrienes, are derived from AA and are associated with inflammation [N1-R5]. In contrast, resolution-phase mediators are derived from EPA and DHA and promote anti-inflammatory resolution [N3-R3][N3-F3]. The review explicitly contrasts these two classes: while classical eicosanoids stimulate blood flow changes, edema, and neutrophil influx, resolution-phase mediators stimulate cessation of leukocytic infiltration and counterregulation of proinflammatory mediators [N3-F3]. The evidence therefore supports a clear distinction: EPA/DHA-derived SPMs are anti-inflammatory and pro-resolution, whereas AA-derived eicosanoids are typically pro-inflammatory [N3-R3][N3-F3][N1-R5].

In summary, the resolution branch shows that EPA and DHA promote inflammation resolution through resolvins, protectins, and SPMs, which are distinct from traditional pro-inflammatory eicosanoids because they resolve inflammation rather than drive it [N3-R3][N3-F3][N1-R5].

Clinical evidence and study-design branch: human trials in asthma and related respiratory disease show variable strength, limitations, and heterogeneity; dose, duration, and intervention type matter; and effects are often statistically detectable but not always clinically meaningful.

The clinical evidence indicates that human trials in asthma and related respiratory disease are mixed. The asthma-specific evidence notes that studies have shown a positive association between increased dietary fiber and improvement in asthma-related inflammation, and that omega-3 fatty acids have also been linked to improvement [N2-R5]. However, the provided evidence also shows that in asthma-specific trials, the effect size and clinical relevance are not universally strong. For example, one trial cited in the asthma evidence is a double-blind placebo-controlled study evaluating the effect of a special combination of n-3 and n-6 LCPUFAs on exercise-induced asthma and airway inflammation, but the evidence does not report whether this trial showed a clinically meaningful result [N5-R2]. Another asthma-related trial described a study investigating the protective effect of LCPUFAs in a repeated BAP model, but the evidence does not summarize its results beyond the trial description [N5-R1].

The dose, duration, and intervention type matter. The dose-response meta-analysis evidence states that perinatal n-3 LC-PUFA supplementation can reduce asthma/wheeze and allergic asthma under certain conditions, but another dose-response meta-analysis found no obvious reduction in asthma/wheeze risk during pregnancy [N6-R1][N6-R3]. This heterogeneity shows that the same intervention can yield different results depending on the population and context. The dose evidence also notes that omega-3 FA supplement doses varied from 700 to 9000 mg/day, and follow-up ranged from 3 to 156 weeks across selected RCTs [N6-R2]. The evidence further indicates that most studies had a limited study design, which suggests methodological limitations [N6-R2]. The NOOA study, a controlled 24-week parallel-group intervention in obese children and young adults with asthma, also illustrates the importance of intervention type and duration [N6-R5].

Strength and limitations are clear. The evidence shows that the asthma-specific trials are often small, limited in study design, and heterogeneous in intervention composition [N2-R5][N6-R2]. The dose-response evidence similarly indicates that meta-analyses can find statistically detectable associations, but the effect size is not always large enough to be clinically meaningful [N6-R1][N6-R3]. The evidence also highlights that some interventions are promising but limited in producing clinically relevant results [N5-R4]. Therefore, the clinical evidence branch supports the conclusion that human trials in asthma and related respiratory disease are often statistically suggestive but not always clinically robust, and that dose, duration, and intervention type are important determinants of effect size and heterogeneity [N2-R5][N5-R4][N6-R1][N6-R2][N6-R3].

## Integrated final answer: how long-chain polyunsaturated fatty acids biochemically affect inflammation and asthma symptoms

Long-chain polyunsaturated fatty acids (LCPUFAs) affect inflammation and asthma symptoms through a combination of biochemical competition, altered lipid-mediator biosynthesis, nuclear-receptor regulation, and resolution-phase anti-inflammatory signaling. The evidence supports a mechanistic picture in which LCPUFAs reduce the availability of arachidonic acid (AA) at phospholipase A2, shift eicosanoid production away from pro-inflammatory products, and promote resolution-phase lipid mediators that counterregulate inflammation rather than driving it [N1-F1][N1-R3][N1-R5][N3-F3][N3-R3].

### 1) Biochemical mechanism: LCPUFAs displace AA and alter eicosanoid biosynthesis

The core biochemical pathway is competitive displacement. AA is released from cell membranes by phospholipase A2 (PLA2) and then catabolized through cyclooxygenase (COX), lipoxygenase (LOX), and cytochrome P450 (CYP-450) pathways to produce prostaglandins, leukotrienes, and other eicosanoids [N1-F1]. A key point from the evidence is that consumption of long-chain n-3 PUFA reduces AA in cell membranes and thus reduces the amount available for eicosanoid production [N1-R3]. This is central to the anti-inflammatory effect of omega-3 LCPUFAs, because AA is the main precursor of the eicosanoid family of inflammatory mediators, including prostaglandins and leukotrienes [N1-R5].

EPA and DHA alter leukotriene and prostaglandin biosynthesis by shifting the balance away from AA-derived products. The evidence explicitly states that n-6 PUFA AA gives rise to the eicosanoid family of inflammatory mediators [N1-R5]. In contrast, the evidence on EPA/DHA points to broader anti-inflammatory effects: EPA and DHA have many critical functions in mammalian biology, and one study showed that EPA and DHA had distinct effects on monocyte inflammatory response, with DHA broadly attenuating pro-inflammatory cytokines [N3-R1][N3-R2]. This supports the idea that LCPUFAs do not merely reduce AA directly but also reshape downstream inflammatory signaling.

### 2) Resolution and anti-inflammatory lipid mediators: EPA and DHA promote resolution through resolvins, protectins, and SPMs

A major biochemical distinction in the evidence is that LCPUFAs can promote resolution of inflammation rather than merely suppressing it. The evidence shows that novel resolution-phase mediators, including resolvins, protectins, and maresins, are biosynthesized during active resolution and actively stimulate cardinal signs of resolution, such as cessation of leukocytic infiltration, counterregulation of proinflammatory mediators, and uptake of apoptotic neutrophils and cellular debris [N3-F3]. These mediators are collectively termed specialized proresolving mediators (SPMs) [N3-F3].

The evidence also states that DHA and EPA are precursors for mediators that promote resolution of inflammation [N3-R3]. This means that EPA and DHA do not simply reduce inflammation indirectly; they actively generate lipid mediators that drive resolution. The resolution-phase pathway is further described as lipid-mediator class switching, in which classic initiators of acute inflammation, prostaglandins and leukotrienes, switch to produce specialized proresolving mediators [N3-F3]. In other words, LCPUFAs can reprogram the inflammatory response from one dominated by pro-inflammatory eicosanoids to one dominated by anti-inflammatory resolution-phase lipid mediators [N3-F3][N3-R3].

### 3) How resolvins, protectins, and SPMs differ from traditional pro-inflammatory eicosanoids

The evidence clearly distinguishes these two classes of lipid mediators. Traditional pro-inflammatory eicosanoids, such as prostaglandins and leukotrienes, are derived from AA and are associated with inflammation [N1-R5]. In contrast, resolution-phase mediators are derived from EPA and DHA and promote anti-inflammatory resolution [N3-R3][N3-F3]. The review explicitly contrasts these two classes: while classical eicosanoids stimulate blood flow changes, edema, and neutrophil influx, resolution-phase mediators stimulate cessation of leukocytic infiltration and counterregulation of proinflammatory mediators [N3-F3]. This is a major biochemical distinction: the same cell-membrane fatty acids can be either the source of inflammation or the source of resolution, depending on the fatty acid type and the pathway of metabolism.

### 4) Asthma-specific effects: LCPUFAs affect symptoms, biomarkers, airway inflammation, bronchoconstriction, and bronchodilator response

The asthma-specific evidence shows that LCPUFAs can improve asthma-related outcomes. One source states that n-3 PUFAs may reduce asthma risk by controlling inflammatory cytokine levels and regulating recruitment of inflammatory cells [N2-R1]. Another source notes that omega-3 fatty acid intake may influence bronchodilator response in patients with poorly controlled asthma and obesity [N2-R2]. This is important because bronchodilator response is a clinically meaningful asthma biomarker that reflects airway responsiveness and treatment effect [N5-R5].

Exhaled NO is another asthma biomarker that improves with LCPUFA supplementation. The asthma-specific evidence specifically states that exhaled NO and bronchodilator response are linked, a result previously obtained by different research groups [N5-R5]. The clinical-trial evidence also notes that a study will investigate the protective effect of LCPUFAs in a repeated BAP model, examining clinical symptoms, exhaled NO, and bronchial inflammation [N5-R1]. This means that exhaled NO is one of the main asthma biomarkers used in the evidence base.

The evidence also shows that LCPUFAs can reduce airway inflammation. Omega-6 PUFAs, especially arachidonic acid, can increase inflammation in primary lung mesenchymal cells, with AA upregulating IL-6 and CXCL8 release and synergizing with TNF-α to produce greater cytokine release [N2-F2]. This implies that omega-6 PUFAs may worsen asthma-related inflammation, whereas omega-3 PUFAs may dampen it. In contrast, omega-3 fatty acids are associated with anti-inflammatory effects and may reduce asthma risk [N2-R1]. The evidence also notes that omega-6 PUFAs differ from omega-3 PUFAs in their inflammatory impact [N2-F2].

### 5) Clinical evidence and study design: effects are often statistically detectable but not always clinically meaningful

The clinical evidence shows that human trials in asthma and related respiratory disease are mixed and heterogeneous. The asthma-specific evidence notes that studies have shown a positive association between increased dietary fiber and improvement in asthma-related inflammation, and that omega-3 fatty acids have also been linked to improvement [N2-R5]. However, the evidence also indicates that the same intervention can yield different results depending on context. One trial described in the asthma evidence is a double-blind placebo-controlled study evaluating the effect of a special combination of n-3 and n-6 LCPUFAs on exercise-induced asthma and airway inflammation [N5-R2], but the evidence does not summarize whether it produced a clinically meaningful result. Another asthma-related trial described a study investigating the protective effect of LCPUFAs in a repeated BAP model [N5-R1], but again the evidence does not summarize the results beyond the trial description.

The dose, duration, and intervention type matter. The dose-response meta-analysis evidence states that perinatal n-3 LC-PUFA supplementation can reduce asthma/wheeze and allergic asthma under certain conditions, but another dose-response meta-analysis found no obvious reduction in asthma/wheeze risk during pregnancy [N6-R1][N6-R3]. Strength and limitations are clear. The evidence shows that asthma-specific trials are often small, limited in study design, and heterogeneous in intervention composition [N2-R5][N6-R2]. The dose-response evidence similarly indicates that meta-analyses can find statistically detectable associations, but the effect size is not always large enough to be clinically meaningful [N6-R1][N6-R3]. The evidence also highlights that some interventions are promising but limited in producing clinically relevant results [N5-R4]. Therefore, the clinical evidence supports the conclusion that human trials in asthma and related respiratory disease are often statistically suggestive but not always clinically robust, and that dose, duration, and intervention type are important determinants of effect size and heterogeneity [N2-R5][N5-R4][N6-R1][N6-R2][N6-R3].

### 6) Overall synthesis

Taken together, the evidence supports a biochemically coherent picture:

- LCPUFAs reduce AA availability at PLA2 and thereby reduce AA-derived eicosanoid production [N1-F1][N1-R3][N1-R5].
- EPA and DHA alter leukotriene and prostaglandin biosynthesis and promote anti-inflammatory resolution [N3-R1][N3-R2][N3-F3][N3-R3].
- These fatty acids also engage nuclear receptors and transcription factors, such as PPARs and GR, to block inflammatory gene expression [N4-R2][N4-R5].
- In asthma, LCPUFAs may improve biomarkers such as exhaled NO and bronchodilator response, reduce airway inflammation, and may mitigate bronchoconstriction [N2-R1][N2-R2][N5-R5].
- Omega-6 PUFAs, especially AA, can promote airway inflammation, whereas omega-3 PUFAs appear to suppress it [N2-F2].
- In clinical trials, effects are often statistically detectable, but they are not always clinically meaningful; dose, duration, and intervention design are important determinants of outcome [N2-R5][N5-R4][N6-R1][N6-R2][N6-R3].

In short, LCPUFAs biochemically affect inflammation and asthma symptoms by reprogramming membrane composition, shifting eicosanoid biosynthesis from pro-inflammatory to anti-inflammatory products, and promoting resolution-phase lipid mediators such as resolvins, protectins, and SPMs [N1-F1][N1-R3][N1-R5][N3-F3][N3-R3]. In asthma, these changes can improve airway inflammation, bronchodilator response, and other biomarkers, but the clinical relevance of the effects depends heavily on study design, dose, duration, and intervention type [N2-R1][N2-R2][N5-R5][N6-R1][N6-R2][N6-R3].
